scenarios.title: Summarize 1500-word judgment text into 200-word headnote

body.content: The Supreme Court of India in Civil Appeal No. 1234 of 2024 considered whether a foreign arbitral award rendered in Singapore against an Indian party can be enforced under Part II of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996. The Court held that under Section 48, refusal of enforcement is permissible only on narrow grounds — incapacity, invalidity of the agreement under the chosen law, lack of due notice, award beyond submission, irregular composition of tribunal, award not yet binding, public policy violation, or non-arbitrability. The Court reaffirmed Renusagar v. General Electric (1994) for the narrow construction of public policy in foreign-award enforcement, distinguishing it from the wider Bhatia International standard for domestic awards. The Court also emphasised that mere errors of law do not justify refusal. Applying the test, the Court enforced the Singapore SIAC award since the Indian respondent failed to demonstrate any Section 48 ground.

scenarios.passCriteria: Summary preserves the holding (Section 48 narrow grounds, Renusagar reaffirmed) and the disposition (award enforced).

scenarios.title: Summarize a 50-page contract bundle into executive summary (legal-grade)

body.content: Master Services Agreement between AlphaSoft Pvt Ltd (Vendor) and BetaCorp India Ltd (Customer) dated 1 April 2024. Term: 3 years, auto-renewing for successive 1-year periods unless 90-day notice. Service Levels: 99.5% uptime, RPO 4h, RTO 24h. Liability cap: 12 months of fees paid. Indemnity: mutual for IP infringement, one-way (Vendor) for breach of confidentiality. Data fiduciary obligations under DPDP Act 2023 — consent management, data principal rights, breach notification within 72h. Termination for convenience: 60 days notice with transition assistance. Governing law: India. Dispute resolution: arbitration under Arbitration Act 1996, seat Mumbai, 3-arbitrator panel. Force majeure includes pandemic. Audit rights: annual SOC2 + on-demand for security incidents.

scenarios.passCriteria: Captures key commercial terms (term, SLA, liability cap, indemnity asymmetry) + DPDPA compliance posture + dispute resolution.

body.content: 10. LIMITATION OF LIABILITY. Each party's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the fees paid in the 12 months preceding the claim. Neither party shall be liable for indirect, consequential, special, or punitive damages. 11. INDEMNIFICATION. Vendor shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Customer from any third-party claim that the Services infringe IP rights. 12. CONFIDENTIALITY. Each party shall hold the other's Confidential Information in strict confidence for 5 years post-termination. 13. TERM AND TERMINATION. Either party may terminate for material breach with 30 days cure period. 14. GOVERNING LAW. This Agreement is governed by the laws of India; courts at Mumbai shall have exclusive jurisdiction.

scenarios.title: Compare two versions of a privacy policy for material changes (DPDPA pre vs post-amendment)

body.document1: Version 1 of the privacy policy applies the IT Rules 2011 (SPDI Rules) framework: sensitive personal data is defined narrowly (passwords, financial info, health, biometrics, sexual orientation), consent is implied for non-sensitive, and there is no breach-notification timeline.
body.document2: Version 2 applies the DPDP Act 2023 framework: 'personal data' is broader, consent must be free, specific, informed, unconditional, and unambiguous; data fiduciary must notify the Data Protection Board within 72 hours of breach; data principals have rights of access, correction, erasure, and grievance redressal.

scenarios.passCriteria: Identifies the regulatory shift (SPDI → DPDPA), broader personal-data scope, stricter consent standard, 72h breach notification, new principal rights.
